How has the role of the musician in society changed from the era of court composers to the age of streaming?

Here's the thing people forget when they romanticize the court composer era: those musicians were literally servants. Haydn had a dress code. Mozart got kicked out — physically kicked — by an archbishop's secretary. The idea that this was some golden age for musicians is wild when you think about who actually got to make music professionally. It was an incredibly tiny number of people, almost all of them dependent on the whims of wealthy patrons who might care deeply about music or might just want background noise for dinner parties.

Every major shift since then has been about more people getting to participate. Public concerts meant musicians could build their own audiences. Recording meant a performer in Memphis or Lagos could be heard worldwide. And now streaming — for all its problems with pay rates, which are real — has blown the doors completely off. A teenager with a laptop and a microphone can put a song in front of millions of people without anyone's permission. No patron, no label executive, no conservatory gatekeeper gets to decide who's worthy.

And the creativity pouring through those open doors is extraordinary. Genres are cross-pollinating in ways that would've been impossible when musicians were siloed by geography and institution. Bedroom producers are inventing sounds that no orchestra could make. The musician's role hasn't been diminished — it's been multiplied. There are more musicians making more kinds of music for more kinds of listeners than at any point in human history. If that's not a golden age, I don't know what is.
What distinguishes a living musical tradition from one that is merely preserved as heritage?

Here's the simplest test: if regular people are still making the music because they want to — not because a grant committee funded it or a university department needs to justify its existence — it's alive. A living tradition is one where someone picks up a fiddle at a kitchen session, where a grandmother teaches a song to a grandchild not as a lesson but just because that's the song you sing while doing that thing. The moment a tradition needs to be officially "preserved," something has already shifted. That doesn't mean preservation is bad — recording, archiving, and teaching endangered musical practices is genuinely valuable work. But there's a world of difference between a tradition that exists in people's daily lives and one that exists primarily on stages and in syllabi. What keeps traditions alive isn't purity or technical rigor — it's use. Bluegrass stays vital because people keep forming bands in garages and playing at local venues, mixing in whatever they've been listening to. The tradition evolves because it belongs to the people playing it, not to a canon. When institutions take over, they often accidentally kill the thing they're trying to save by insisting on "correct" versions and proper techniques, turning something that was communal and messy and joyful into something you need credentials to participate in. The most alive traditions are the ones that don't even think of themselves as traditions — they're just what people do. They absorb new influences shamelessly, they adapt to new instruments and new contexts, and nobody's checking whether you have permission to join in.
Is the Western canon of great music a genuine achievement to be studied, or an artifact of cultural power?

Here's what always gets me about the 'great canon' conversation: we're told these are the greatest musical achievements in human history, and then you find out that the list was basically assembled by a handful of European music critics, conservatory directors, and concert promoters over the last two centuries. That's not a universal judgment — that's a very specific tradition deciding it's the main tradition. Think about what the canon leaves out. Centuries of extraordinary music-making across the globe — the melodic sophistication of West African griot traditions, the rhythmic complexity of Afro-Cuban music, the improvisatory genius of delta blues, the harmonic inventiveness of Brazilian popular music — none of this was considered 'serious' enough to study. Meanwhile, every conservatory student had to master the same European repertoire as if it were the only path to musical understanding. And within Europe itself, the oral traditions, the folk musicians, the dance music that actually filled people's lives — all dismissed as lesser. The canon isn't really about identifying the best music ever made. It's about one particular culture's way of valuing certain kinds of complexity — written-down complexity, specifically — over other kinds. A bluegrass fiddler or a flamenco guitarist possesses a depth of musical knowledge that's just as real as anything in a symphony score, but it was never going to make the canon because it lived in bodies and communities rather than on paper. I'm not saying Bach isn't brilliant — he clearly is. I'm saying that calling a specific list of European composers 'the canon' and then asking everyone else to justify their music against that standard is a pretty neat trick.
How does the experience of learning about a musical tradition through study compare to growing up immersed in it?

Here's the thing that drives me a little crazy about this debate: you can study the blues for twenty years in a university, transcribe every Robert Johnson recording, write a dissertation on blue notes and AAB lyric structures — and still not swing. Meanwhile, someone who grew up with that music in their bones, who heard it at family gatherings and church and on the porch, knows something about it that no textbook can teach.

That's not anti-intellectual — it's just honest about what music actually is. Music isn't a text to be decoded. It's a living practice, a way of being in the world with other people. When you grow up inside a tradition, you don't just learn the notes — you learn what the music is for, when it's appropriate, how it breathes, what it means to the people who make it. You learn the jokes, the references, the feeling of a room when a song hits right.

Study has its place, sure. Learning theory can open doors, and there's nothing wrong with curiosity about traditions that aren't your own. But let's not pretend that someone with a PhD in a musical tradition automatically understands it better than the grandmother who's been singing those songs her whole life. Too often, academic study becomes a way of claiming authority over something that belongs to the people who live it every day.

The most honest musicians I know — the ones who cross into traditions they weren't born into — will tell you straight up: you never fully get there from the outside. You can get close, you can contribute beautifully, but that bone-deep knowing? That comes from living it.
What is the relationship between a culture's investment in musical education and the quality of its musical output?

Here's the thing about this question — it smuggles in an assumption that I think we need to challenge. The idea that formal musical education produces 'better' music is one of those claims that sounds reasonable until you actually look at the history of music that has moved people most deeply.

The Delta blues came from one of the least formally educated musical communities imaginable, and it literally reshaped the sound of the entire world. Hip-hop was born from DJs and MCs with no conservatory training, using turntables and drum machines, and it became the most influential musical movement of the last fifty years. Jamaican sound system culture, punk rock, electronic dance music — some of the most explosive creative movements in music history came from people who were told they didn't have the 'proper' training to make real music.

I'm not anti-education — music classes in schools are wonderful, and learning an instrument can be a beautiful experience. But the idea that a culture's musical output improves in proportion to its investment in formal training confuses one very specific kind of music-making with music itself. What actually produces vibrant musical cultures is access to instruments and tools, communities where people make music together, and the freedom to experiment without being told you're doing it wrong.

Some of the most heavily funded classical music institutions in the world are producing technically flawless performances that audiences are steadily abandoning. Meanwhile, a teenager with a laptop and genuine feeling is making something that connects with millions. Maybe 'quality' isn't about how many people passed their grade eight exams. Maybe it's about whether the music is alive — whether it makes people feel something, dance, sing along, or see the world differently. That kind of quality doesn't require a curriculum. It requires a culture that lets people play.
How should we think about the tension between accessibility and artistic standards in presenting music to new audiences?

I think we need to question the whole framing here, because it assumes that 'artistic standards' and 'accessibility' are naturally opposed — and that's doing a lot of sneaky work. Who set these standards? Who decided that complexity equals quality, that difficulty equals depth? Usually it's the people who already have access, drawing a line behind them and calling it a standard. Here's what I've noticed: every time someone makes music more accessible — whether it's a YouTuber breaking down orchestral works, a DJ remixing classical themes, or a venue ditching the dress code — the gatekeepers panic. They say standards are falling. But what's actually happening is that more people are engaging with music on their own terms, and that terrifies anyone whose authority depends on being the expert in the room. The truth is, most of the music we now consider 'high art' was popular entertainment in its day. Mozart wrote crowd-pleasers. Verdi was the blockbuster filmmaker of his era. The idea that serious music must be difficult and exclusive is a relatively recent invention. And honestly? Some of the most innovative, emotionally powerful music being made right now lives on SoundCloud and Bandcamp and TikTok, created by people with no formal training who are just following their ears and their hearts. Instead of worrying about maintaining standards, we should be asking: are people connecting with music? Is it moving them, inspiring them, bringing them together? If the answer is yes, then the music is doing its job. Everything else is just credentialism.
What does the decline of music criticism in major publications suggest about the role of expertise in cultural life?

Honestly? I think the decline of traditional music criticism tells us something that critics themselves would rather not hear: most people never needed a professional intermediary to tell them what was worth listening to.

That sounds harsh, but think about it. For decades, a handful of critics at a handful of publications wielded enormous influence over what got attention and what didn't. They had genuine knowledge, sure, but they also had massive blind spots — entire genres dismissed, whole traditions ignored because they didn't fit the frameworks these writers were trained in. How many years did major publications treat hip-hop as a fad? How long did it take for critics to catch up to what electronic music producers were doing?

What we have now isn't a void — it's an explosion. Music discourse is thriving in fan communities, on YouTube channels run by obsessive enthusiasts, in Reddit threads where people debate mixing techniques and song structures with incredible specificity. The knowledge didn't disappear; it just stopped being funneled through a tiny bottleneck of credentialed voices.

And here's what I think gets overlooked: the best music writing happening today is often more passionate and more detailed than what appeared in legacy publications, precisely because the people writing it are doing so out of love rather than professional obligation. A fan who's spent ten years deep in a genre often has insights that a generalist critic parachuting in for a review simply can't match.

Expertise matters — but expertise was never limited to people with press credentials. The real shift isn't the death of knowledge about music. It's the death of the idea that knowledge needs a gatekeeper.
How do changing technologies of music reproduction reshape what counts as an authentic musical experience?

Every time a new music technology comes along, someone declares that real musical experience is dying. The phonograph was going to kill live music. Home taping was killing music. MP3s were killing music. Streaming is killing music. And yet — more people are making, sharing, and deeply loving music right now than at any point in human history. That tells you something. The whole idea that authenticity requires a concert hall, or a pristine vinyl pressing, or some ritualized form of deep listening is really just a way of saying that your way of experiencing music is the right one. But think about a teenager in a small town who discovers Coltrane through a Spotify recommendation, or a bedroom producer in Lagos who builds an entire sound world on a laptop, or someone who finds the exact song they need during a hard moment because an algorithm surfaced it. Are those experiences less authentic? I'd argue they're profoundly authentic — music meeting people exactly where they are, in their real lives, on their own terms. Technology hasn't degraded the musical experience; it's multiplied the doorways into it. Sure, the formats change, and listening habits shift. But the core thing — a human being moved by organized sound — that hasn't changed at all. If anything, removing the gatekeepers and the expensive equipment and the geographic barriers has made authentic connection with music more possible, not less. The most authentic musical experience is the one that actually reaches you.
